episode_thesis: Two days after the November 2024 US election, Alan Dunne and Niels Kaastrup-Larsen read the clean Republican sweep as a policy-expectations shock (tax cuts, deregulation, tariffs as a bargaining chip) that lifted equities and Treasury yields while current US data stayed solid, with the unsustainable deficit as the main risk to yields. They treat Goldman's 3% ten-year S&P forecast and the concentration warning as plausible but unproven, and argue that in an unpredictable policy environment systematic, forecast-free strategies such as trend following (despite a bad October when bonds, equities and the dollar reversed together) belong in portfolios.

speakers.name: Alan Dunne
speakers.role: Dublin-based macro and systematic investor and co-host who runs the Global Macro series; co-host of the Systematic Investor series
speakers.speaker_note: Captions spell him 'alen Don'. He carries most of the macro and election analysis and the paper reviews in this episode. Ledger claims that name 'Alan' only are the same person.

worldview_premises.premise: Relative national economic strength moves in long cycles: Germany once led and Ireland now has fiscal surpluses and full employment; Europe's problems are policy paralysis plus demographics and weak productivity, so the bullish European case is hard to make.
worldview_premises.support: Personal observation (Germany versus Ireland over his lifetime) and current news (Volkswagen cuts, German coalition split).

worldview_premises.premise: Narratives are built after the fact to fit any data point, and polls again underestimated Trump support; incumbents are being voted out worldwide after a post-inflation period, with grocery prices the dominant theme.
worldview_premises.support: Poll misses in 2024, the late-weekend Harris swing narrative, and global incumbent losses.

worldview_premises.premise: The markets had expected a Trump win but not a clean sweep; the rally reflects expectations of policy (supply-side optimism) rather than the current economy.
worldview_premises.support: Betting odds of 55 to 66% for Trump; falling oil and copper alongside rising equities and yields.

worldview_premises.premise: The US economy in late 2024 is solid (consumption, services ISM strongest since mid-2022, core PCE sticky but falling on six-month basis), with labour-market softening looking like rebalancing; the labour market is lagging but could turn if firms cut hiring sharply.
worldview_premises.support: Data points cited from the latest releases.

worldview_premises.premise: Tariffs are a one-off price-level effect and probably a bargaining chip, so the Fed can look through them if expectations stay anchored.
worldview_premises.support: Textbook reasoning plus the 2019-2020 US-China deal precedent; he admits he has a wait-and-see opinion.

worldview_premises.premise: The US deficit trajectory is unsustainable and will not be reduced much whoever wins, so yields have upside risk; the resolution is either a bond-vigilante fiscal crisis or a political shift.
worldview_premises.support: Consensus among his macro guests; no model offered.

worldview_premises.premise: Long-horizon forecasts agree that US equity returns will be below the last decade's, and high index concentration historically precedes higher volatility and lower ten-year returns; valuation depends on margins and bond yields.
worldview_premises.support: Goldman's report, with JPM, AQR and GMO as other examples; Goldman's own track record may undershoot.

worldview_premises.premise: Bond expected return equals the starting yield held to maturity, and bonds provide stability and convexity in a large equity sell-off; trend following or managed futures is the better diversifier when bonds are doubtful, and buffer ETFs are not.
worldview_premises.support: Instrument mechanics; his past work on structured products.

worldview_premises.premise: Investors extrapolate recent returns, which is why alternatives are hard to sell, even though the last decade's equity gains rested on real earnings growth and not on speculation alone.
worldview_premises.support: Bloomberg report on alternative sales; earnings history.

worldview_premises.premise: Sell-side houses are normally bullish, so a pessimistic Goldman forecast is notable, though it could be a sales pitch for alternatives.

Systematic strategies are spreading in multi-asset portfolios and across asset classes, and adding an alternative that trades assets already held needs a more nuanced efficient-frontier analysis than simple combination.
worldview_premises.support: Invesco 2024 survey (factor tilting 80%, rotation models 67%, trend 44%, vol targeting 41%, AI 90%).

mechanism_chains.topic: How the election result reached asset prices

steps.from: Clean Republican sweep (both houses, with reconciliation available)
steps.to: Expectations of tax cuts, deregulation and supply-side policy
steps.why: Two years of near carte blanche, moderated by the McConnell faction.

steps.to: Higher growth without higher inflation, so equities rally
steps.why: The supply-side idea is that policy raises aggregate supply.

steps.to: Treasury yields rise (60 to 70bp since the 50bp Fed cut)
steps.why: A mix of growth repricing and deficit concern.

steps.to: Rally reflects expectations, not current demand
steps.why: A usual reflation cycle would also lift cyclical commodities.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Cross-asset moves in the days after the election and recent data.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Moderate Republicans block spending and tax cuts; tariffs prove permanent and inflationary; the deficit forces a bond-market crisis.

steps.to: A one-off rise in the price level
steps.why: Inflation is a rate of change, not a level.

steps.to: The Fed may look through it
steps.why: As long as inflation expectations stay anchored.

steps.to: A US-China deal as in 2019-2020
steps.why: Bluster and a bargaining chip, though not ruled out as permanent.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Reasoning plus precedent; Alan states 'wait and see'.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Tariffs become broad and permanent, or Fed independence is undermined (Bessent's shadow Fed chair idea).

mechanism_chains.topic: Deficits, bond vigilantes and the yield path

steps.from: Unsustainable US spending and deficit trajectory
steps.to: Upside risk to long yields over time
steps.why: Nearly every macro guest agrees; deficits are unlikely to shrink regardless of election result.

steps.to: Long yields rose from that day (an own goal for the aim of lower yields)
steps.why: The curve reacted to growth and fiscal expectations.

steps.from: Bessent as Treasury secretary, or large Musk-identified savings
steps.to: Deficit could fall to about 3%, easing yield risk
steps.why: He favours a strong dollar and deficit reduction.

steps.to: A fiscal crisis enforced by bond vigilantes, or a political shift
steps.why: Resolution has to come one way or another.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Guest consensus, yield moves; one strategist's view that the 10-year could pass 5%.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: A 1990s-style Clinton-Greenspan deal (deficit reduction for easier policy) happens, which he calls implausible.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why concentration lowers expected index returns (Goldman)

steps.to: Hard to keep growing earnings at 7 to 10%
steps.why: The economy is only so big; these firms are already a large share.

steps.to: Rested on 7% earnings growth, lower taxes, higher margins and multiple expansion (PE from 16 to 22)
steps.why: These cannot all repeat.

steps.to: 3% nominal ten-year S&P forecast and equal weight 2 to 8% better
steps.why: Equal weight forecast is about 8%, normal.

steps.to: Bonds likely to beat equities
steps.why: Expected bond return is the yield held to maturity.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Goldman's report; other houses' low forecasts.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Mega-cap moats, cash and AI investment let concentration and earnings growth persist.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why diversification should favour alternatives and trend following

steps.to: Trend following with Sharpe 0.4 to 0.5 at 12% vol plus 3% cash gives 7 to 8%
steps.why: Compares favourably with both.

steps.from: Rising yields and doubts about bonds
steps.to: A diversifier with convexity is needed
steps.why: Bonds offered stability and convexity in sell-offs; buffer ETFs only cover 10 to 15% of decline and cap the upside; short duration lacks convexity.

steps.to: Alternatives are hard to sell anyway
steps.why: The S&P is doing 15% a year.

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Access to trend products is difficult for retail investors, as noted.

decision_process.practice: Read long-horizon forecasts (Goldman, JPM, AQR, GMO) and compare their assumptions on margins, bond yields, concentration and recession frequency rather than the headline number.
decision_process.why: The swing variable is concentration; the macro scenario is mild (four contraction quarters in 10 years).

decision_process.practice: Check an earlier model's forecast track record (Goldman's ten-year-old model undershot).
Use trend following or managed futures as the stabiliser alongside or instead of bonds; shorten bond duration if trend is inaccessible; be cautious about buffer ETFs.
decision_process.why: Convexity in a sell-off is the bond role to replace.

decision_process.practice: When adding alternatives to a 60/40, consider that they may trade the same assets already held, so exposures overlap.
decision_process.why: A nuance to the efficient frontier approach; his planned blog post.

decision_process.practice: Evaluate macro events through expectations (what markets price for policy) rather than current data alone.
decision_process.why: Rally in equities and yields reflected Trump-era policy, not trajectory of data.

speakers.evidence_style: Current data points and releases, recalled guest conversations (Ferman, Moran and others), published reports (Goldman, Invesco), instrument mechanics and historical analogies (1990s Clinton-Greenspan, 2019-2020 trade deal). Mostly narrative reasoning with explicit hedges ('wait and see').

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.role: Host of Top Traders Unplugged and veteran hedge fund manager; trend following specialist
speakers.speaker_note: Captions spell him 'Neil Castro blon'. In this episode he asks many questions but also states views on the election, trend following's October, and Goldman's forecast, so he is mapped. The ledger correction to the October claim (equities were a third losing leg) is applied.

worldview_premises.premise: Low-probability outcomes occur, and inflation was largely a COVID-era shock (with Fed mistakes) that the Democrats did not rebut; money and polls do not decide elections (Harris out-raised Trump by about $1.2bn).
Independent long-form podcasts are an influential medium, which mainstream media and the Harris campaign underused; Musk's role helps US competitiveness against Europe.
worldview_premises.support: His own listening to a long podcast interview; reasoning.

worldview_premises.premise: EU bureaucracy of 27 countries slows decisions and hurts competitiveness.

Policy uncertainty makes forecasting market reactions from discretion or reading economic reports harder, which favours systematic, no-prediction strategies; the core edge is being systematic, doing what the model says.
worldview_premises.support: Fifty years of evidence at his firm (referenced); no new data.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend followers lose big when the three big financial sectors (bonds, equities, currencies) all turn against positions at once, regardless of how diversified the portfolio is; fixed income is also the main correlation driver.

Old-school mechanics (higher yields and inflation must hurt equities) have not held, and higher rates may help cash-rich mega-caps; index leadership changes over time, so concentration's return effect is unclear even if volatility rises.
worldview_premises.support: S&P strength in 2023-24; Nvidia's rise as the example.

worldview_premises.premise: The equity bull market may end in a parabolic move, possibly triggered by the election.
worldview_premises.support: Hunch he says he has held 'for a while'.

mechanism_chains.topic: October 2024: why trend followers had a bad month

steps.from: Bond exposure flipped from short to long around June-July and was built up into the Fed meeting
steps.to: Managers were long when fixed income peaked at the Fed cut and sold off
steps.why: The trend signal was long going into the turning point.

steps.from: The dollar, sold against many currencies, suddenly strengthened; other equity markets fell
steps.to: Currency and equity trends also reversed
steps.why: All three big financial sectors moved against positions at once.

steps.from: Medium-term lookbacks did worse than faster and slower ones
steps.to: Whipsaw in the sweet spot of many CTAs
steps.why: Alan adds that bond moves were large enough to flip signals but reversed.

steps.to: Possible renewed trend traction
steps.why: Trends may resume with policy direction clearer.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Index performance data (BTOP50 +1.91% YTD, SG CTA -0.78%, SG Trend about -2%, short-term traders down about 1% in the month) and manager lookback data.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: If one sector (such as the longer-term trend in equities) had offset the loss; Lean Hogs' great month did not offset.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why Goldman's bonds-beat-equities call is hard to accept for Niels

steps.from: Higher inflation and yields did not damp equities
steps.to: Rate-based valuation mechanics are unreliable
steps.why: The S&P did well; cash-rich firms such as Apple may even gain from higher rates.

steps.to: Today's top 10 may not be the top 10 in 10 years
steps.why: Concentration implies volatility but not clearly lower returns.

steps.to: Doubts bonds will beat equities
steps.why: Conflicts with his mental model; but as a trend follower he need not be right.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Market behaviour in 2023-24 and reasoning; he repeatedly says he is 'thinking out loud'.

decision_process.practice: Track trend-following performance by sector and by lookback speed (medium-term worse than fast or slow in October 2024) and compare the main indices (BTOP50, SG CTA, SG Trend, short-term traders).
decision_process.why: Explains dispersion and which sector hurt.

decision_process.practice: Do not forecast: follow the model's trend signals through policy uncertainty.
decision_process.why: Systematic strategies avoid the need to be right on forecasts like Goldman's.

speakers.evidence_style: Observation, index numbers for the month, and personal anecdote (travel to West Palm Beach, listening to a podcast). Little formal analysis.

disagreements.topic: Will bonds beat equities over the next decade, and does concentration lower equity returns?

positions.speaker: Alan Dunne
positions.position: Goldman's logic is plausible: with the 10-year near 4% bonds are likely to beat a 3% equity forecast, and concentration has historically meant lower returns; valuation and yields point to below-average returns, while noting moat and AI counterarguments.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Doubts bonds beat equities given his inflation view, thinks concentration raises volatility but its effect on returns is unclear because index leaders change and cash-rich firms may benefit from higher rates; adds he need not decide as a trend follower.

disagreements.topic: Do higher yields and inflation justify lower equity valuations?

positions.speaker: Alan Dunne
positions.position: Higher yields would in themselves justify lower valuations and reversion to the mean, though he accepts that reversion has been expected for a long time.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: The old mechanic did not hold in 2023-24; the S&P rose and cash-rich mega-caps may benefit from higher rates.

disagreements.topic: Which sector explains October's trend-following losses?

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: All three big financial sectors (bonds, equities and currencies) turned together, so a diversified portfolio still lost.

positions.speaker: Alan Dunne
positions.position: Fixed income was the swing variable across managers because moves were long enough to flip positions and then reversed.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Attribution of the post-election yield rise is mixed: 'deficit concerns' (C08-2) versus 'growth repricing from lower taxes and deregulation' (C08-X1); the share of each is not estimated.
The tariff view is a hunch ('wait and see'); both a one-off price effect and a bargaining-chip outcome are asserted without evidence on scale or duration.
The statement that US recession risk peaked in August 2024 and faded is not backed by data in the episode; labour-market softening is read both as rebalancing and as a possible harbinger.

Trend following expected return of 7 to 8% uses an assumed Sharpe of 0.4 to 0.5, 12% vol and 3% cash; the Sharpe assumption is not evidenced, and 2024 year-to-date returns in the same episode are far below it.
The parabolic equity move comment is a hunch with no mechanism or trigger beyond the election.

Goldman's call that bonds beat equities is compared as yield to maturity versus a 3% forecast; risk, reinvestment and inflation differences are not discussed, and Alan says its model undershot ten years ago.
Medium-term lookbacks underperforming in October is reported from data Niels 'has access to', without a number; the explanation (whipsaw) is offered by both speakers without a test.
Claims about the election (poll misses, podcasts, Musk's role, RFK Jr) are political commentary with no market evidence; the Musk $26.5bn net-worth gain is a one-day move cited as proof of repricing.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs named as leading prices: the US labour market (hiring and layoffs) for recession risk; services ISM, consumption and core PCE (six-month annualised) for growth and disinflation; Fed path (JPM now expects cuts every other meeting, ending near 3.5%); Treasury yields and the deficit path (reconciliation, Bessent, Musk's cost cutting, 60 or 70bp rise since the cut, possible 5% 10-year); tariff announcements and any US-China deal; index concentration, valuations (PE 16 to 22), margins and bond yields for the ten-year equity forecast; and for trend followers the three big sectors moving together and bond position changes. Horizons: weeks for trend and yields, two years for the policy window, ten years for Goldman's forecast.
reader_inferences: (reader) Both speakers treat the post-election rally as a story about expected policy, not data, which implies it is fragile to the first sign that tax cuts, tariffs or spending cuts are diluted; neither states what would falsify it.

(reader) Alan's argument for trend following is arithmetic (expected return versus 4% bonds and 3% equities) plus convexity, while Niels's is epistemic (no need to forecast); the two justify the same allocation for different reasons.

(reader) The October trend loss is explained by all sectors reversing at once, which implies that diversification across the big three financial sectors fails when macro regime turns, and that the remaining diversification must come from smaller sectors, shorter horizons or non-price signals.

(reader) Alan's distinction between price-level and inflation-rate effects of tariffs is the basis for his Fed look-through expectation; it breaks if expectations unanchor, which is the observable to watch.
